London AI × Science Hackathon · Protein Engineering Track · 3–4 October 2026

Can protein foundation models
predict peptide–HLA stability?

Structure prediction, inverse folding and protein language models — tested against a sequence-only baseline, on HLA alleles the model has never seen.

Introduction

Which peptides stay bound to which HLA?

HLAs show the immune system what's inside the cell

Class I HLAs hold short peptide fragments (typically 8–11 amino acids) in a groove on the cell surface for T-cell surveillance. Different alleles bind different peptides, so personalised immunotherapy needs a ranking of which peptides bind which allele.

We predict stability, not affinity

Stability is how long a peptide stays in the groove once bound — largely the off-rate. The target is the measured half-life in hours, from the NetMHCstabpan dataset: 28,166 measurements, 75 alleles, all 9-mers.

Can foundation models beat sequence-only?

The standard approach, NetMHCstabpan, is a supervised model on peptide–HLA sequence pairs. We ask whether three kinds of protein foundation model add to it:

Structure prediction Boltz-2, Chai-1Inverse folding LigandMPNNLanguage models ESM-2

Can inverse folding
predict peptide–HLA stability?

Predict how long a peptide stays bound to an HLA class I molecule — for alleles the model has never seen. We asked whether LigandMPNN's structural knowledge helps.

Method

Four setups, one shared architecture

① Frozen LigandMPNN

HLA threaded onto 5 peptide–HLA templates × 3 decoding orders. Scores each 9-mer — no labels used.

50 features: 1 mean log-prob · 9 per-position log-probs · 40 anchor (P2/P9) probs

→

② Supervised baseline inputs

Peptide: BLOSUM50, 9×20
Allele: 34-residue pseudosequence, one-hot 34×20

+ ①'s 50 features, concatenated, for setups 3 & 4

→

③ MLP head

64 → 32 hidden units, same fixed optimizer and 20-epoch budget for every setup.

Output: log half-life (MSE) — ranking loss as exploratory follow-up.

Conclusion

Structural information helps — as an added feature

0.423 → 0.493
Geometry adds what sequence misses

The baseline sees only sequence. Adding features from the 3D pocket lifts held-out-allele Spearman by +0.07 — roughly a third more of the ranking explained.

59 / 75
Consistent across alleles

Nearly four in five unseen alleles improve. The gain is broad, not carried by a handful of alleles.

0.130 → 0.035
The signal is pocket-specific

Scramble the HLA sequence in the same structure and the zero-shot score collapses — the score depends on the real pocket sequence in its structural context.

Scope: fixed-budget, single-seed comparison. The structure model also sees more of the HLA (182 vs 34 residues), so gains are not yet isolated to geometry alone.
